analysis.one_liner: Requires for-profit colleges to get at least 15% of revenue from non-federal student aid.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal student aid like Pell Grants and federal loans is the main revenue source for many for-profit colleges. Existing law already requires these schools to get at least 10% of their revenue from other sources — the so-called 90/10 rule. This bill would raise that bar to 15%, meaning a for-profit college that draws more than 85% of its money from federal aid would lose access to that aid, pushing students toward schools less dependent on federal dollars.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges and federal taxpayers. Students would be less likely to enroll at schools kept afloat almost entirely by federal aid — schools that historically have had weak outcomes — and taxpayers would stop subsidizing tuition at colleges that generate no revenue beyond federal checks.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Higher Education Act to require for-profit colleges to derive at least 15% of their revenue from non-federal sources, up from 10%, or lose eligibility for title IV federal student aid [S2][S3].
The rule would apply starting with the 2018-2019 award year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges that rely on federal student aid for most of their revenue would lose that revenue or exit federal aid programs, and some of their students would need to find other schools.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges dependent on federal aid

drawbacks.text: For-profit colleges serve many working adults and low-income students; schools pushed out of federal aid programs by the higher threshold could close, leaving enrolled students scrambling to finish their programs elsewhere.

The bill is a one-word change to the existing threshold; it does not close known workarounds, such as revenue from other federal programs (for example veterans' benefits) that historically did not count toward the federal-share limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The change is modest and targeted: it tightens an existing accountability rule rather than creating a new program, and its main effect would fall on schools whose business model depends almost entirely on federal student aid. The real costs fall on a concentrated industry, with some risk to enrolled students at marginal schools. The bill does nothing about loopholes in how the rule is measured, so its practical bite could be smaller than the numbers suggest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the 85/15 Rule Act in the House on May 25, 2017 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
No committee action followed: no cosponsors joined, and the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that depend on federal student aid for most of their revenue kept the looser 10% threshold, and no vote was ever held on the stricter rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges reliant on federal aid

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it to the House, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; the bill died there without a hearing or vote
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, so it never advanced to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a single Democrat with no cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-led committee it was assigned to never acted on it.

industries.note: Many for-profit schools collect most of their revenue from federal student aid; the bill raises the minimum non-federal share from 10% to 15%, which would cut off title IV aid to schools above 85% federal revenue and shrink their federal-funded tuition stream.
